topics.title: Linear graphs
topics.html:
y = mx + c
  • m = gradient, c = y-intercept
  • Gradient = riserun = y₂ − y₁x₂ − x₁
  • Positive m slopes up ↗, negative slopes down ↘
  • Horizontal line y = a: gradient 0. Vertical line x = a: gradient undefined
  • Parallel lines have the same gradient
ExampleThrough (1, 3) and (4, 9): m = 6 ÷ 3 = 2. 3 = 2(1) + c → c = 1, so y = 2x + 1.
Watch out: rearrange into y = … before reading m. In 2y = 6x − 4, the gradient is 3, not 6.

Vertical line x = a : gradient undefined Parallel lines have the same gradient Example Through (1, 3) and (4, 9): m = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 . 3 = 2(1) + c → c = 1 , so y = 2 x + 1 . Watch out: rearrange into y = … before reading m . In 2 y = 6 x − 4, the gradient is 3, not 6.

topics.title: Expansion
topics.html:
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²

General: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd (multiply every term by every term).

Example(2x − 3)² = 4x² − 12x + 9
Watch out: (a + b)² ≠ a² + b². Don't forget the middle term 2ab. Also watch the sign: −(x − 4) = −x + 4.
topics.text: ( a + b )² = a ² + 2 ab + b ² ( a − b )² = a ² − 2 ab + b ² ( a + b )( a − b ) = a ² − b ² General: ( a + b )( c + d ) = ac + ad + bc + bd (multiply every term by every term). Example (2 x − 3)² = 4 x ² − 12 x + 9 Watch out: ( a + b )² ≠ a ² + b ² . Don't forget the middle term 2 ab . Also watch the sign: −( x − 4) = − x + 4 .

topics.title: Factorisation
topics.html:
Try these in order:

  • Common factor: 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)
  • Special products: x² − 25 = (x + 5)(x − 5)
  • Grouping: ax + ay + bx + by = (a + b)(x + y)
  • Quadratic x² + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b (multiplication frame or cross method)
Examplex² − x − 12: −4 × 3 = −12 and −4 + 3 = −1, so (x − 4)(x + 3).
2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3)
Watch out: factorise completely. 2x² − 18 = 2(x² − 9) = 2(x + 3)(x − 3). Check by expanding back.
topics.text: Try these in order: Common factor: 6 x ² + 9 x = 3 x (2 x + 3) Special products: x ² − 25 = ( x + 5)( x − 5) Grouping: ax + ay + bx + by = ( a + b )( x + y ) Quadratic x ² + bx + c : find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b (multiplication frame or cross method) Example x ² − x − 12 : −4 × 3 = −12 and −4 + 3 = −1, so ( x − 4)( x + 3) . 2 x ² + 7 x + 3 = (2 x + 1)( x + 3) Watch out: factorise completely. 2 x ² − 18 = 2( x ² − 9) = 2( x + 3)( x − 3) . Check by expanding back.

topics.title: Algebraic fractions
topics.html:
• Simplify: factorise top and bottom, then cancel common factors
  • Add / subtract: use the LCM of the denominators
  • Multiply: factorise, cancel, then multiply across
  • Divide: flip the second fraction, then multiply
Examplex² − 9x² + 3x = (x + 3)(x − 3)x(x + 3) = x − 3x
Watch out: you can only cancel factors, never terms. x + 3x ≠ 3.
topics.text: Simplify: factorise top and bottom, then cancel common factors Add / subtract: use the LCM of the denominators Multiply: factorise, cancel, then multiply across Divide: flip the second fraction, then multiply Example x ² − 9 x ² + 3 x = ( x + 3)( x − 3) x ( x + 3) = x − 3 x Watch out: you can only cancel factors, never terms. x + 3 x ≠ 3 .

topics.title: Changing the subject
topics.html:
Undo operations in reverse order, doing the same thing to both sides. If the new subject appears twice, collect those terms on one side and factorise it out.

ExampleMake r the subject of V = πr²h:
r² = Vπh → r = √Vπh
Exampleax + b = cx → x(a − c) = −b → x = bc − a
topics.text: Undo operations in reverse order, doing the same thing to both sides. If the new subject appears twice, collect those terms on one side and factorise it out. Example Make r the subject of V = πr ² h : r ² = V πh → r = √ V πh Example ax + b = cx → x ( a − c ) = − b → x = b c − a

topics.title: Quadratic equations & graphs
topics.html:
Solve by factorisation: rearrange to … = 0, factorise, then set each factor to 0.

(x − p)(x − q) = 0 ⇒ x = p or x = q

Graph of y = ax² + bx + c:

  • a > 0: ∪ shape with a minimum point. a < 0: ∩ shape with a maximum point
  • y-intercept = c. x-intercepts = the roots
  • Line of symmetry sits halfway between the roots: x = p + q2
Examplex² − 5x = −6 → x² − 5x + 6 = 0 → (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 → x = 2 or 3
Watch out: never divide both sides by x. In x² = 4x that loses the answer x = 0. Write x(x − 4) = 0.
topics.text: Solve by factorisation: rearrange to … = 0 , factorise, then set each factor to 0. ( x − p )( x − q ) = 0 ⇒ x = p or x = q Graph of y = ax ² + bx + c : a > 0 : ∪ shape with a minimum point. a < 0 : ∩ shape with a maximum point y -intercept = c . x -intercepts = the roots Line of symmetry sits halfway between the roots: x = p + q 2 Example x ² − 5 x = −6 → x ² − 5 x + 6 = 0 → ( x − 2)( x − 3) = 0 → x = 2 or 3 Watch out: never divide both sides by x . In x ² = 4 x that loses the answer x = 0 . Write x ( x − 4) = 0 .

topics.title: Simultaneous equations
topics.html:
• Elimination: make one variable's coefficients equal, then add or subtract the equations
  • Substitution: make one variable the subject, then substitute into the other equation
  • Graphical: the solution is the point where the two lines intersect
Examplex + y = 10 … (1)   x − y = 4 … (2)
(1) + (2): 2x = 14 → x = 7, then y = 3.
Watch out: check both values in the other equation. Parallel lines give no solution.
topics.text: Elimination: make one variable's coefficients equal, then add or subtract the equations Substitution: make one variable the subject, then substitute into the other equation Graphical: the solution is the point where the two lines intersect Example x + y = 10 … (1) x − y = 4 … (2) (1) + (2): 2 x = 14 → x = 7 , then y = 3 . Watch out: check both values in the other equation. Parallel lines give no solution.

topics.title: Linear inequalities
topics.html:
Solve like an equation, with one extra rule:

× or ÷ by a negative ⇒ flip the sign

Filled dot ● for ≤ or ≥. Open dot ○ for < or >.

Example5 − 2x > 11 → −2x > 6 → x < −3
Watch out: "largest integer x" for x < −3 is −4, not −3.

topics.title: Congruence & similarity
topics.html:
Congruent (same shape, same size). Tests for triangles:

SSS · SAS · AAS (ASA) · RHS (RHS: right angle, hypotenuse, side)

Similar (same shape, different size): corresponding angles equal and corresponding sides in the same ratio.

ABPQ = BCQR = ACPR = k

Two triangles with two pairs of equal angles are similar (AA).

Watch out: name vertices in matching order. △ABC ≡ △PQR means A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. SSA and AAA do not prove congruence.

Area scale = (length scale)²

topics.title: Pythagoras' theorem
topics.html:
a² + b² = c²

c is the hypotenuse, the longest side, opposite the right angle.

Converse: if a² + b² = c², the triangle is right-angled.

Common triples: 3‑4‑5, 5‑12‑13, 8‑15‑17, 7‑24‑25 (and their multiples).

Watch out: finding a shorter side means subtracting: a = √(c² − b²).
topics.text: a b c a ² + b ² = c ² c is the hypotenuse, the longest side, opposite the right angle. Converse: if a ² + b ² = c ² , the triangle is right-angled. Common triples: 3‑4‑5, 5‑12‑13, 8‑15‑17, 7‑24‑25 (and their multiples). Watch out: finding a shorter side means subtracting: a = √( c ² − b ²) .

topics.title: Trigonometric ratios
topics.html:
sin θ = opphyp   cos θ = adjhyp   tan θ = oppadj

Remember TOA CAH SOH. Use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ to find an angle.

Examplehyp = 10, θ = 30°: opp = 10 sin 30° = 5.
Watch out: calculator must be in DEG mode. Label opp/adj from the angle you are using. They swap for the other angle.

topics.title: Statistical diagrams
topics.html:
• Dot diagram: one dot per value on a number line. Good for small data sets
  • Stem-and-leaf: keeps every value. Always include a key, e.g. 3 | 4 means 34. Leaves in ascending order
  • Histogram: for grouped continuous data. Bars touch, and equal class widths are used in Sec 2
Stem-and-leaf 2 | 3 5 8
3 | 0 4 4 9
4 | 1 6    Key: 3 | 4 = 34
Watch out: spot misleading graphs: axes not starting at 0, uneven scales, or 3‑D pictures that exaggerate size.

topics.title: Mean, median, mode
topics.html:
Mean = sum of valuesnumber of values = ΣfxΣf
  • Median: middle value after sorting. Position n + 12. If n is even, average the two middle values
  • Mode: most frequent value (can be none, or more than one)
  • Grouped data: use class mid-values for x. The answer is an estimate
Example3, 7, 7, 9, 14: mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8, median = 7, mode = 7.
Watch out: an extreme value (outlier) pulls the mean. The median is better then. Sort the data before finding the median.

topics.title: Probability
topics.html:
P(E) = number of favourable outcomestotal number of outcomes
  • 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. Impossible = 0, certain = 1
  • P(not E) = 1 − P(E)
  • List the sample space (all outcomes) when unsure. For two dice there are 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes
ExampleBag of 3 red and 5 blue: P(red) = 38, P(not red) = 58.
Watch out: give answers as fractions in simplest form (or decimals), never as ratios like 3 : 8.
